\chapter{Capitals, Short Forms And Symbols}
\label{ch:mayusculas-abreviaturas}
\hlchaptermodality{426}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can keep days, months, languages and nationalities lower-case the way Spanish does, tell an abbreviation from an initialism from a symbol by whether it takes a point, and read a filled-in form line by line.}

Read a completed personal-details form, saying each short form aloud in full and explaining why each lower-case word is lower-case.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[las mayúsculas]{las mayúsculas — and the four things Spanish refuses to capitalise}

\label{lesson:ES-C426-mayusculas}



\begin{quote}
Write today's day and month in English. Now write them in Spanish, and read on to find out what you almost certainly got wrong.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la mayúscula} — \textquotedblleft{}the capital letter.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{La minúscula} is the small one. Latin \emph{maiusculus}, \textquotedblleft{}somewhat larger,\textquotedblright{} and \emph{minusculus}, \textquotedblleft{}somewhat smaller\textquotedblright{} — the two names describe nothing but size.

Spanish capitalises where you expect: the first word of a sentence, and proper names — people, cities, countries, rivers.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the four that English capitalises and Spanish does not}]
This is the highest-value fact in the chapter, because an English-trained hand gets all four wrong and the marker sees every one:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{English} & \textbf{Spanish} \\
\midrule
days & Monday & \textbf{lunes} \\
months & January & \textbf{enero} \\
languages & Spanish & \textbf{español} \\
nationalities & I am Spanish & soy \textbf{español} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Add religions and titles: \emph{católico}, and \emph{el rey}, \emph{el presidente}, \emph{doctor} — all lower-case in running text.

The idea underneath is consistent. Spanish capitalises a \textbf{name}, not a \textbf{category}. \emph{España} is a name; \emph{español} is a description of a kind of person, and a description is an ordinary adjective.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the title of a book or a film}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
English & \emph{One Hundred Years of Solitude} \\
Spanish & \emph{Cien años de soledad} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Only the first word takes a capital. English capitalises most words in a title; Spanish treats a title as an ordinary sentence with a capital at the front.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item today's day and month in Spanish, both lower-case
  \item \textquotedblleft{}soy español\textquotedblright{} and hear that the nationality is not capitalised
  \item the single rule underneath all four (a name is capitalised, a category is not)
  \item how many words of a Spanish book title take a capital (one)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does Spanish capitalise \emph{lunes}? (No.) Does it capitalise \emph{España}? (Yes.) What is the difference? (A name takes a capital; a category does not.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la minúscula inicial]{la minúscula inicial — the capital that depends on what stands beside it}

\label{lesson:ES-C426-minuscula-inicial}



\begin{quote}
Say the principle from the last lesson: a name takes a capital, a category does not. This lesson gives you a case where the same word takes a capital in one sentence and not in another.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
Many Spanish surnames contain a small word: \textbf{de}, \textbf{del}, \textbf{la}, \textbf{las}. Whether it is capitalised depends on \textbf{what stands in front of it}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{written} & \textbf{form} \\
\midrule
with the first name & Pedro \textbf{de} la Cruz \\
without it & el señor \textbf{De} la Cruz \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

With the forename present, the small word is lower-case. Standing alone at the head of the name, it takes the capital.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: why the rule has that shape}]
It is not arbitrary. \textbf{De} originally meant \emph{from} — \emph{Pedro de la Cruz} was Pedro \textbf{from} the Cross, a description of where he came from rather than a name. A description does not take a capital, which is the rule from the last lesson exactly.

Once the forename is gone, \emph{De la Cruz} has become the whole name, and a name takes a capital.

This appears on forms. A field asking for \emph{apellidos} alone is the second row; a field with \emph{nombre y apellidos} together is the first.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Pedro de la Cruz\textquotedblright{}, and say which word is lower-case
  \item the same surname without the forename, and say what changed
  \item what \emph{de} originally meant, and why that explains the rule
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is it \emph{Pedro De la Cruz} or \emph{Pedro de la Cruz}? (Lower-case \emph{de}, because the forename is there.) And with no forename? (\emph{De la Cruz}, capital.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[las abreviaturas]{las abreviaturas — the short forms a letter opens with}

\label{lesson:ES-C426-abreviaturas}



\begin{quote}
You know that \textbf{c/} on an address is \emph{calle}. Say it. That slash was your first abbreviation; this lesson gives you the rest of the set.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{una abreviatura} — \textquotedblleft{}an abbreviation\textquotedblright{}: a word written short, and \textbf{always closed with a point}.

The forms of address are the ones an A1 paper prints:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{short} & \textbf{full} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
Sr. & señor & Mr \\
Sra. & señora & Mrs \\
Srta. & señorita & Miss \\
D. & don & a courtesy title before a first name \\
Dña. & doña & its feminine \\
Dr. & doctor &  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The point is not decoration. \textbf{Sr} without it is an error, because the point is what marks the word as shortened.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: don and señor are not the same word}]
The distinction is one an English speaker has no equivalent for:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{goes before} & \textbf{example} \\
\midrule
señor & the \textbf{surname} & el Sr. García \\
don & the \textbf{first name} & D. Pedro \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Don Pedro} is respectful and warm; \emph{Señor García} is respectful and formal. Putting them the wrong way round — \emph{don García} — sounds wrong to a Spanish ear in the way \emph{Mr. Peter} does to an English one.

Two more an address prints, both of which you can now read: \textbf{c/} for \emph{calle} and \textbf{n.º} for \emph{número}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the abbreviations for \emph{señor}, \emph{señora} and \emph{señorita}
  \item what must never be left off the end of an abbreviation (the point)
  \item which of \emph{don} and \emph{señor} goes with a first name
  \item what \textbf{c/} and \textbf{n.º} stand for
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What closes every abbreviation? (A point.) Which goes before a first name, \emph{don} or \emph{señor}? (\emph{Don}.) What is \emph{Dña.} short for? (\emph{Doña}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[las letras voladitas]{las letras voladitas — the little letters that sit above the line}

\label{lesson:ES-C426-voladitas}



\begin{quote}
Say the abbreviation for \emph{señora}. Now say what you would write for \emph{señorita} if you wanted the raised form, and read on.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{las letras voladitas} — \textquotedblleft{}the flown letters,\textquotedblright{} raised above the line. Spanish uses exactly two of them, \textbf{º} and \textbf{ª}, and which one you use is decided by gender.

Their commonest job is the \textbf{ordinal indicator}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{written} & \textbf{read} \\
\midrule
1.º & primero \\
1.ª & primera \\
2.º & segundo \\
n.º & número \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English writes \emph{1st} and \emph{2nd}, changing the ending with the number. Spanish writes the same raised letter every time and changes it only for \textbf{gender}: \textbf{º} for a masculine word, \textbf{ª} for a feminine one.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the point goes before the raised letter}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{correct} & \textbf{wrong} \\
\midrule
1.º & 1º \\
Sr.ª & Srª \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The Academy's recommendation puts the \textbf{point first and the raised letter after}, because the point is the abbreviation mark and the raised letter is the ending. You will see the pointless form printed everywhere; the one with the point is the one to write.

A warning about the shape. \textbf{º} is a raised letter \textbf{o}, not a degree sign, even though the two look nearly identical. A temperature uses the degree sign; an ordinal uses the letter.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item 1.º and 1.ª, and say what decides between them
  \item where the point goes relative to the raised letter
  \item what \textbf{n.º} stands for
  \item the difference between the raised \textbf{º} and a degree sign
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What decides between \textbf{º} and \textbf{ª}? (The gender of the word.) Does the point come before or after the raised letter? (Before.) Is \textbf{º} a degree sign? (No — it is a raised letter o.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[las siglas]{las siglas — no points, and a plural made by doubling}

\label{lesson:ES-C426-siglas}



\begin{quote}
Say the rule you learned for abbreviations: every one ends in a point. This lesson gives you a kind of short form where that rule is reversed.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{una sigla} — a set of initials standing for a name. \emph{ONU}, \emph{DNI}, \emph{RENFE}.

Unlike an abbreviation, \textbf{a sigla takes no points at all}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{correct} & \textbf{wrong} \\
\midrule
DNI & D.N.I. \\
ONU & O.N.U. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The two you will actually meet on a form are \textbf{DNI} — \emph{Documento Nacional de Identidad}, the Spanish identity card — and \textbf{UE}, the European Union.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the plural, which is the strange part}]
A sigla does \textbf{not} take an \textbf{-s} in writing. It is made plural by \textbf{doubling its letters}, with a space in the middle:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{singular} & \textbf{plural} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
EU & \textbf{EE. UU.} & the United States \\
CC & \textbf{CC. OO.} & a trade union confederation \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{EE. UU.} is \emph{Estados Unidos} — two words, so two doubled letters. Said aloud it is the full name; the doubling exists only on the page.

One more distinction the names record. A \textbf{sigla} is spelled out letter by letter (\emph{DNI} is \emph{de-ene-i}). An \textbf{acrónimo} is said as a word (\emph{RENFE}, \emph{ONU}). Which one a set of initials becomes depends on nothing but whether the result is pronounceable.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{DNI}, spelled out with the letter names you learned
  \item whether a sigla takes points (no)
  \item how \emph{Estados Unidos} is written short (\emph{EE. UU.})
  \item the difference between a \emph{sigla} and an \emph{acrónimo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does a sigla end in a point? (No — an abbreviation does, a sigla does not.) How is a sigla made plural in writing? (By doubling its letters.) What does \textbf{DNI} stand for? (\emph{Documento Nacional de Identidad}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[los símbolos]{los símbolos — the third kind of short form, and the one with no point}

\label{lesson:ES-C426-simbolos}



\begin{quote}
An abbreviation ends in a point and a sigla does not. Say both rules. This lesson adds a third kind, and it sides with the sigla.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{un símbolo} — a fixed sign for a unit, a currency or a direction. It is \textbf{international, unchanging, and takes no point}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{symbol} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
€ & the euro \\
km & kilometre \\
kg & kilogram \\
h & hour \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{km} is never \emph{km.} and never \emph{kms}. A symbol has no plural and no point, because it is not a shortened Spanish word — it is the same sign in every language.

You have already read one in use: \textbf{km/h}, which you learned to say aloud as \emph{kilómetros por hora}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the compass, and where the euro goes}]
The four points of the compass have symbols that match their Spanish names, and one does not match the English:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{symbol} & \textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
N & norte & north \\
S & sur & south \\
E & este & east \\
\textbf{O} & \textbf{oeste} & west (\textbf{W}) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

A Spanish map prints \textbf{O} where an English map prints \textbf{W}. On a reading paper that is a trap worth having seen once.

And the currency: Spanish writes the amount first and the symbol after, with a space — \textbf{20 €}, not \emph{€20}. English does the reverse.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item whether a symbol takes a point (no)
  \item the four compass letters in Spanish, and the one that differs from English
  \item \textquotedblleft{}20 €\textquotedblright{} the way Spanish writes it, and say what English would do instead
  \item the plural of \emph{km} (there is none)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the three short forms takes a point — abbreviation, sigla or symbol? (Only the abbreviation.) Which compass letter differs between Spanish and English? (\textbf{O} for \emph{oeste}, where English writes \textbf{W}.) Where does the euro sign go? (After the amount.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tres formas cortas]{tres formas cortas — and the point tells you which is which}

\label{lesson:ES-C426-repaso-cortas}



\begin{quote}
Name the three kinds of short form before reading on, and say which one takes a point.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one test separates all three}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{kind} & \textbf{example} & \textbf{point?} \\
\midrule
abreviatura & Sr., Dña., n.º & \textbf{yes} \\
sigla & DNI, ONU, UE & no \\
símbolo & €, km, N & no \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The reason is worth more than the table. An \textbf{abreviatura} is a Spanish word cut short, and the point marks the cut. A \textbf{sigla} is not a cut word but a set of initials. A \textbf{símbolo} is not Spanish at all — it is an international sign that happens to appear in a Spanish sentence.

Only something that was cut needs a mark showing where.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the capitals, gathered}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{lower-case in Spanish} & \textbf{capitalised} \\
\midrule
lunes, enero & España, Madrid \\
español, católico & Pedro, García \\
el rey, el doctor & De la Cruz, with no forename \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

One idea covers the whole left column: \textbf{a category is not a name.} Days, months, languages, nationalities, religions and titles all describe a kind of thing rather than naming a particular one.

And the raised letters: \textbf{º} for a masculine word, \textbf{ª} for a feminine one, with the point \textbf{before} — 1.º, 1.ª, Sr.ª.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three kinds of short form, and which takes a point
  \item four things Spanish leaves lower-case that English capitalises
  \item why an abbreviation needs a point and a symbol does not
  \item 1.ª, and say what the raised letter is agreeing with
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the three takes a point, and why? (The abbreviation — the point marks where the word was cut.) What single idea keeps \emph{lunes} and \emph{español} lower-case? (They are categories, not names.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[un formulario completo]{un formulario completo — where all of it actually turns up}

\label{lesson:ES-C426-sintesis-formulario}



\begin{quote}
Say what \textbf{DNI} stands for, and say whether it takes points.
\end{quote}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
Read this form. Every short form in it has been taught:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Datos personales} Nombre y apellidos: Pedro de la Cruz DNI: 12345678-A Dirección: c/ Mayor, n.º 5, 1.º Teléfono: 600 123 456 Correo electrónico: Nacionalidad: español
\end{quote}

Six things to notice, and every one is a rule rather than a detail: \emph{de la Cruz} is lower-case because the forename is present; \textbf{DNI} carries no points; \textbf{c/} is the street and \textbf{n.º} the number; \textbf{1.º} is the floor, with the point before the raised letter; and \textbf{español} is lower-case because a nationality is a category.
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the same data spoken aloud}]
A form prints the short forms; a person says them in full:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{on the form} & \textbf{said aloud} \\
\midrule
c/ Mayor & calle Mayor \\
n.º 5 & número cinco \\
1.º & primero \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

A reading paper gives you the left column and a listening paper the right, which is why both have to be learned.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the address line of the form, aloud and in full
  \item your own nationality, and keep it lower-case
  \item \textbf{DNI}, letter by letter, using the Spanish letter names
  \item why \emph{de} is small in \emph{Pedro de la Cruz}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why is \emph{español} lower-case on the form? (A nationality is a category, not a name.) How is \textbf{1.º} read aloud? (\emph{Primero}.) Where does the point go in \textbf{n.º}? (Before the raised letter.)
\end{tcolorbox}
